gloss.6: to stop; at first a footprint

ming.title: 名: a name is also a reputation
ming.body: 名 is the plain word “name”. The Shuowen explains the graph as 夕, evening, above 口, a mouth: in the dark people cannot see each other, so each one calls out who they are. In the Warring States the word had grown large. 名 was a person’s reputation, and it was also rank and title, the name by which a court knew and paid a man. The wandering advisers of the time lived by it. A good name opened the gate of a ruler; a ruined one closed every gate. English must choose “name”, “fame”, or “reputation”. We keep “name” because the first line of the book uses the same word: the name that can be named. A name is a sound in the mouths of others. Where is it kept?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 口部: 名，自命也。从口从夕。夕者，冥也。冥不相見，故以口自名。

shen.title: 身: the body, not “life”
shen.body: The Shuowen says of 身: 象人之身, “it pictures a person’s body”. The graph is commonly explained as a figure seen from the side with the trunk drawn large; some see a pregnant belly, and 身 still means “pregnancy” in the phrase 有身. The word covers the trunk, the whole body, and the person: 身 is how classical Chinese says “oneself”. English translators often write “life” or “self” here, and both are too thin. The question is physical. Fame is in the mouths of others, and this is in your skin. The book returns to the word often. Passage 13 says that great trouble comes from having a 身, and then gives the world to the one who values the body as the world. Passage 26 asks how a lord of ten thousand chariots can treat the body more lightly than the realm.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 身部: 身，躳也。象人之身。

qin.title: 親: near, kin, dear
qin.body: 親 is one word where English has three. It means near in space, it means parents and relatives, and it means dear. The Shuowen defines it with one syllable: 至也, “it arrives”, it comes all the way to you. The graph has 見, to see, on the right: the people whom you see every day. So the first question does not ask which of the two is “better” or “more valuable”. It asks which is closer kin. The answer looks easy, and the text gives none. The question had [[a school behind it|yangzhu]]. In a court society the honest answer was often the name: men died to protect it, and families lived on it for generations. The question measures a distance. How far from you is your reputation, and how far is your hand?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 見部: 親，至也。从見亲聲。

huo.title: 貨: shells that change hands
huo.body: 貨 is 貝, a cowrie shell, under 化, to change. The Shuowen glosses it 財也, “wealth”, and treats 化 as the sound. Under 貝 the same dictionary keeps a short history of money: 古者貨貝而寶龜, “the ancients used shells as goods and treasured tortoise shell”; the Zhou had coins, and the Qin ended the shell. Cowries came from distant seas and are found in Shang tombs. By the Warring States, bronze money in the shapes of spades and knives moved between the states, and great merchants grew rich on salt and iron. 貨 is wealth in that form: things that can be carried, priced, and exchanged. The book is wary of it. Passages 3, 12, and 64 all speak of 難得之貨, “rare goods, hard to come by”, and of what such goods do to people.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 貝部: 貨，財也。从貝化聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 貝部: 貝，海介蟲也。… 古者貨貝而寶龜，周而有泉，至秦廢貝行錢。

duo.title: 孰多: which is “more”?
duo.body: 多 means “much, many”. Here it is the measure: of body and goods, which is the greater amount? The word is exact for the topic. Goods are the things that people count, and the line asks you to put the body on the same scale. A story told in the Zhuangzi and in the Lüshi Chunqiu makes the test concrete. Master Zihua asks a lord of Han, who is at war over a strip of land: suppose a document said that whoever takes it gains the world and loses a hand. Would you take it? The lord says no. Then, says Zihua, your two arms count for more than the world, and your body for more than your arms; and the land that you fight for counts for much less. We render “counts for more”; “is worth more” would also do.
src: Zhuangzi, “Rang wang” (讓王)
Lüshi Chunqiu, “Shen wei” (審為)

de-wang.title: 得與亡: gain and loss of what?
de-wang.body: The third question names no objects. 得 is to get and 亡 is to lose, or to be gone. Gain of what, and loss of what? One reading takes the line alone: is it getting or losing that harms a person? Common sense says loss, and the passage then argues that getting is the sickness. [[Wang Bi|wangbi]] reads the line as the sum of the first two: to gain name and goods and to lose the body. A third reading reverses it: gain the body and lose the rest. The Chinese holds all three, because it does not say whose gain it is. The rendering adds no objects. Note the sound: 得 is said like 德, the “inner power” of the book’s title, and early texts often explain 德 as 得, “to get”. The word 亡 returns in the fifth line as the fate of the hoard.
src: Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 44

bing.title: 病: sickness, not “worse”
bing.body: 病 is illness. The Shuowen: 疾加也, “a sickness that has grown heavy”. As a verb it means to make ill, to distress, to find fault with. Many translations write “which is worse?” or “more harmful”, and the image is lost. The first two questions used words of measure: nearer, more. The third changes to medicine. It asks for a diagnosis. The answer is not obvious to the patient, because this sickness feels like health: the store grows, the name grows. Passage 71 uses the word in the same way and makes a remedy from it: 病病, to be sick of the sickness, is to be free of it. The left and top part of the graph, 疒, marks illnesses; the Shuowen explains it as a person who leans on a bed.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 疒部: 病，疾加也。从疒丙聲。

ai.title: 愛: to love and to grudge
ai.body: 愛 has two old senses, and the line uses both. It is to love, to hold dear. It is also to be sparing with a thing, to grudge it. In the Mencius a king sees an ox on its way to be killed for a rite and orders a sheep in its place. The people, Mencius tells him, 皆以王為愛也: “all took Your Majesty to be stingy”. The word there is 愛. So 甚愛必大費 says: extreme love must cost greatly. It also says: the extreme miser must pay greatly. 費 is to spend and to waste; it has 貝, the cowrie, at its foot. English “attachment” brings in modern psychology, and “love” alone misses the miser. Notice that the line has no object. It does not say love of what. Is there a love that does not hold on?
src: Mencius 1A7

cang.title: 多藏必厚亡: the storehouse and the tomb
cang.body: 藏 is to store and to hide. The Shuowen gives one word: 匿也, “to conceal”. A reader of the time would think of two places. One is the treasury. The states of this period fell one after another, and a full storehouse was a reason for an attack. The other place is the grave; 厚, “thick”, the word for the loss in this line, is also the usual word for a lavish burial, 厚葬. The rich were buried with bronzes, jade, lacquer, and silk, and tomb robbery was already an old trade. The Heshang Gong commentary reads the line across both: goods in the storehouse bring raiders in life, and goods in the grave bring diggers after death. There is an irony for us. This very line survives in its oldest copy because it was stored in a tomb at Guodian, about 300 BCE, and robbers had opened that tomb shortly before the archaeologists came in 1993. See [[the old copies|variant]].
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 艸部: 藏，匿也。
Heshang Gong commentary on Laozi 44

zhizu.title: 知足: to know the foot
zhizu.body: 足 is “foot”, and it is also “enough”. The two are one graph and one syllable; how the second sense came from the first is not settled. So 知足, “to know enough”, can be seen as “to know the foot”: to know where you stand. The phrase runs through the book. Passage 33: 知足者富, “who knows enough is rich”. Passage 46: 知足之足常足, “the enough of ‘know enough’ is always enough”, with three 足 in six characters. English “contentment” makes it a feeling. The Chinese makes it knowledge: an accurate sense of a quantity. It is also not “settle for less”. The line does not say how much is enough. It says that there is such a point, and that it can be known. See the plate for [[足|zu-zhi]].
src: Laozi 33, 46

zu-zhi.title: 足 and 止: two feet in two lines
zu-zhi.body: Look at the two characters together. 足 has 止 inside it: the Shuowen analyses it as 从止、口, from 止 and 口. And 止, “to stop”, is commonly explained as the picture of a foot or footprint. The Shuowen itself notes the link: 故以止爲足, “so 止 is used for the foot”. The couplet therefore puts a foot in each line. Enough is a foot. Stopping is a foot. The image under both is a person who stands still on the ground. The sound joins them too. In the old rhyme groups, 足 rhymes with 辱 in its own line, and 止 rhymes with 殆 in the next and with 久 at the close. Mandarin still keeps the first pair, zú and rǔ; it has lost the second.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 足部: 足，人之足也。在下。从止、口。
Shuowen Jiezi, 止部: 止，下基也。象艸木出有址，故以止爲足。

zhizhi.title: 知止: the skill of stopping
zhizhi.body: Passage 32 has the same promise: when names have been made, know to stop, and there is no danger. Stopping sounds like the absence of a skill. Try it today and see. Stop a meal one bite before full. End a talk one sentence before the last point that you wanted to add. Close the work when it is done and not when you are tired. In each case you will find a moment when enough has arrived, and a pull to go past it. The pull is the 甚 of the fourth line, “extreme, too much”. Do not fight it. Only learn to recognise the moment just before it. What does “enough” feel like in the body, one second before “more”?

ru.title: 辱: shamed at the edge of the field
ru.body: 辱 is public disgrace. The Shuowen explains the graph with a scene from the farming year: 从寸在辰下。失耕時，於封畺上戮之也, “from 寸 under 辰. One who missed the time of ploughing was punished on the boundary mound.” 辰, it adds, is 農之時, “the farmer’s season”. So the dictionary’s disgrace is the shame of bad timing, displayed where the neighbours could see. Modern scholars read the picture in another way; see the plate. In either case 辱 is social: it is done to you in front of others. That fits the audience. A man at a Warring States court could lose rank, be mutilated, or be killed with his kin when his name or his wealth grew too visible. The book pairs 辱 with 寵, favour, in passage 13: both arrive like a shock.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 辰部: 辱，恥也。从寸在辰下。失耕時，於封畺上戮之也。辰者，農之時也。

dai.title: 殆: danger with bones in it
dai.body: 殆 is “danger”; the Shuowen says 危也. Its left part is 歹, written 歺 in the dictionary: broken bone, the sign of death and harm. It stands in 死, to die, and in 殘, to maim. The right part, 台, gives the sound. The word is the usual one for mortal risk in the texts of the time. Sunzi’s most famous line uses it: know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles there is no 殆. The Laozi uses the same two words, 不殆, five times. Once they describe the Way itself, which goes round and is not imperilled (25). In the other four the cause of safety is not strength. It is a kind of knowing: to know the constant (16), to know to stop (32 and here), to know the mother’s child and keep to the mother (52).
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 歺部: 殆，危也。从歺台聲。
Sunzi, “Mou gong” (謀攻)

changjiu.title: 可以長久: what lasts?
changjiu.body: The last line has no subject. 可以 is “can thereby”; 長 is long and 久 is lasting. English wants to know who or what lasts: you, your life, your house, your state? The rendering says “it” and leaves the place open. Read with the first line, the answer is the body: a long life. Read at a court, it is the family line and the state. Passage 7 gives the model: 天長地久, “heaven is long and earth is lasting”, and they last because they do not live for themselves. Note the size of the promise. The passage does not offer wealth, peace of mind, or success. It offers two absences, no disgrace and no danger, and time. Is that a small reward or a large one?
src: Laozi 7

wangbi.title: Wang Bi: things that cannot pass through
wangbi.body: Wang Bi answers each question in one line. On the first: 尚名好高，其身必疏, “exalt the name and love height, and the body must grow distant.” On the second: 貪貨無厭，其身必少, “crave goods without limit, and the body must count for less.” His two adjectives, 疏 (distant) and 少 (less), are the exact opposites of 親 and 多. On the fourth and fifth lines: 甚愛不與物通，多藏不與物散，求之者多，攻之者眾，為物所病. “Extreme love does not let things pass through; much storing does not let things disperse. Those who seek it are many, and those who attack it are a crowd; one is made sick by things.” His verbs are 通, to flow through, and 散, to scatter. The fault for him is the blockage. A thing that is loved too much is taken out of circulation.
src: Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 44

yangzhu.title: Yang Zhu and the party of the body
yangzhu.body: The first two questions sound like a school of the fourth century BCE that later lost its books. Its teacher was Yang Zhu. Mencius attacks him in a famous line: Yang would not pull out one hair to benefit the whole world. Other sources are kinder. The Huainanzi sums up his teaching as 全性保真，不以物累形: “keep your nature whole, protect what is genuine, and do not let things burden the body.” Chapters of the Lüshi Chunqiu with titles such as “Value Life” and “The Self is Weighty” argue the case in full. In a time when rulers spent bodies freely, in armies and in labour on walls, to say that one body outweighs goods and office was a political statement. The Laozi shares the premise, and it was Yang’s kind of question that [[Legge|legge]] turned into a hymn. Its conclusion is different: it turns the care of the body into the test of who may hold the world (13).
src: Mencius 7A26
Huainanzi, “Fan lun” (氾論訓)

legge.title: Legge sings it
legge.body: Legge saw that this passage rhymes, and he put it into English rhymed verse: dear, adhere, near; shame, blame. It was an honest attempt, and it shows the cost. The three questions of five characters each become seven lines. 身 becomes “life”, and the body goes. 病 becomes “sorrow and pain”, the language of a Victorian hymn. For the fourth line he writes that the one who cleaves to fame “rejects what is more great”: he has supplied an object, fame, for a line that has none, and the double sense of [[愛|ai]] goes too. The close, “Long live shall he”, adds a “he” that the Chinese does not have. Read the Chinese count aloud instead: five, five, five; then six and five; then four, four, four.
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

variant.title: Among the oldest lines we have
variant.body: This passage is on the Guodian bamboo slips, the oldest known copy of Laozi material, buried about 300 BCE. It is nearly the same as the text of five centuries later. The Mawangdui silk texts, buried in 168 BCE, are reported to differ in one small place: they have no 是故 before the fourth line and put 故, “so”, before 知足: 多藏必厚亡 故知足不辱. The conclusion is then drawn one step later: the cost and the loss are stated as facts, and the “so” belongs to the advice. The Guodian slips are reported to read the fifth line with the two adjectives exchanged, “thick storing, much loss”. The sense is the same. The three questions have stood unchanged for some twenty-three centuries.
src: Mawangdui Laozi (collated reconstruction; not checked against silk A or B)
Guodian Laozi A

pair-gain-loss.title: 得/亡: the store and the loss arrive together
pair-gain-loss.body: The passage asks about pairs and gives no answers: name or body, body or goods, [[getting 得 or losing 亡|de-wang]]. Then it shows how one side of the last pair makes the other. Much stored, 多藏, and heavy loss, 厚亡, are one event seen at two times; a person with no store cannot lose it. Extreme love and great cost are joined in the same way. So the text does not say that gain is bad and loss is good. It says that each is carried inside the other, and that 甚, “extreme”, is the point where the turn starts. The passage favors “enough” and “stop”. That is advice for those who have a name and a store, in courts where both were deadly. It turns as well: “enough” held as a rule is a new store, and a name for wanting little is still a name. What have you lost that left you with more?

lenses.ground: Three questions of five characters each, all on one frame: A 與 B 孰 C, “A or B, which is more C?” [[Name|ming]] or [[body|shen]], which is [[nearer|qin]]? Body or [[goods|huo]], which is [[more|duo]]? [[Gain or loss|de-wang]], which is the [[sickness|bing]]? The body stands in the first two and is the hinge between them. No answer is given. Then two laws, each with 必, “must”: great love, great cost; much stored, heavy loss. Then two short rules of four characters, built on [[two words for the foot|zu-zhi]]: know enough, know to stop. The reward is stated last and it is modest: [[it can last|changjiu]]. The passage has no Dao, no heaven, and no sage. It is addressed to a person who has a name and a store, and something to lose.
lenses.inner: The questions do not work as rhetoric. Ask them slowly and something moves. Which is nearer, the name or the body? The name is made of other people’s thoughts; no one has ever met their own reputation. The body is here before the question is finished. Yet most of a day’s worry goes to the first. The passage does not say that the name is bad. It asks about distance, and a person can check the distance directly. The same test applies to [[love|ai]]. The line does not tell you to love less. It observes that 甚, the extreme degree, turns love into a grip, and that a grip is tiring to hold. [[Know enough|zhizu]] is then not a rule of restraint. It is what remains when the nearer thing is felt as nearer.
lenses.leading: A person who leads is paid in [[名|ming]] and [[貨|huo]]: title and reward. The passage speaks to that person. In the courts of the time, [[disgrace|ru]] and [[danger|dai]] were concrete, and they came most often to those who had risen far and stored much. The warning still holds for a house, a company, a team. An organisation that loves one thing to the extreme, a product, a founder, a number, will pay any cost to keep it, and the cost appears elsewhere. [[Wang Bi|wangbi]] names the mechanism: the loved thing stops moving. And the hoard, of cash, of data, of authority, brings the many who seek it. [[The skill of stopping|zhizhi]] is a hard one for the successful, because each earlier step past “enough” was rewarded.
lenses.body: Put the passage where it points: in the [[body|shen]]. Stand up. [[足 and 止|zu-zhi]] are both feet. Let the weight go down into the soles until the two feet are fully on the floor. This is the physical sense of “enough”: nothing leans forward to the next thing. In movement arts, the one who reaches too far gives away the centre, and the hand that grips hard cannot feel. Extreme love of the win costs the balance: 甚愛必大費. Try a slow reach for an object and stop at the point where the back foot would lift. That point is 知止. Past it you are in [[殆|dai]]: you can be pulled. Before it you can stay as long as you like.
lenses.practice: Ask the three questions about one real thing today, and answer in writing. A message that you want to send to defend your [[name|ming]]: name or body, which is nearer? A purchase, or an extra hour of paid work at night: body or [[goods|huo]], which counts for more? A gain that you have chased for a month: is the gain or the loss the [[sickness|bing]]? Then do the small exercise of [[stopping|zhizhi]] once. Do not make a rule from it. The passage gives none; it gives questions, two observations, and the word [[enough|zhizu]].

plates.title: The foot that means “enough”
plates.lesson: Two parts, one above the other. The top is 口, which in most characters is a mouth. Here it is not a mouth: it is commonly explained as what is left of the knee or the lower leg, a round shape in the old forms. The bottom is 止, and that is the foot itself. 止 alone is commonly explained as a footprint, the sole with its toes; it came to mean “to stop”, the place where the foot rests. The Shuowen keeps both facts: 足 is 人之足也。在下。从止、口, “a person’s foot; it is below; from 止 and 口”. Look for 止 in other characters and you find feet everywhere. 步, a step: the Shuowen analyses it as two 止 turned opposite ways, left foot and right foot. 正, upright, has it at the base. As a side part, 足 is squeezed to 𧾷 and marks what legs do: 路 (road), 跪 (to kneel), 跳 (to jump), 踐 (to tread). Then the second meaning: enough, sufficient, to be worth. No one is sure how the foot came to carry it. In this passage the pair is the whole teaching: [[知足, 知止|zu-zhi]]. A foot above a foot. The character for “enough” is a person who has come to a stand.
plates.brush: Seven strokes. The first three make 口: the left side down, then the top and the right side in one stroke with a corner, then the base. Keep this box small and a little flat; it is the knee and not the main part. The fourth stroke is a vertical from the middle of the box’s base. The fifth is a short horizontal that goes out to the right from the middle of that vertical. The sixth is a stroke that falls to the left. Watch the seventh: a long stroke that begins near the sixth, travels down to the right, presses, and lifts into a sharp tail. It runs far past the box on the right, and it is the ground on which the character stands. In seal script the lower part is still a clear 止. In cursive the bottom becomes one turning line.

plates.title: A hand and a hoe
plates.lesson: The top is 辰 and the bottom is 寸. Take the bottom first. 寸 is “inch”: the Shuowen explains it as the spot one inch back from the hand where the pulse moves, and analyses it as 又, a hand, with one mark. In compounds it usually means only “hand”: 守 (to guard), 封 (to raise a boundary mound), 得 (to get), which stands in this passage. Now the top. 辰 is today the fifth of the twelve branches and a word for a time or a star. The Shuowen calls it 農之時, the farmer’s season. Many modern scholars explain the old form as a farm tool, a hoe or a blade made from a large clam shell; the basis is the family of characters around it. 農, farming, has 辰 below. 蜃 is a great clam. 耨, to weed, has 辱 itself on the right. So 辱 is commonly explained as a hand that holds the hoe: to weed, to work the soil. How did it come to mean [[disgrace|ru]]? The Shuowen answers with its story of the late ploughman punished at the field’s edge. Others think the word “shame” only borrowed the graph for its sound. This is disputed; hold both. Its cousin 恥, shame, is glossed by the Shuowen with this character: 恥，辱也.
plates.brush: Ten strokes: seven for 辰, three for 寸. 辰 begins with a horizontal, then a long stroke that falls to the left and makes a roof with it, like the cliff shape 厂. Under that roof come two more horizontals, the second one longer. The fifth stroke goes down and flicks up to the right. The sixth is a short stroke to the left, and the seventh is a long one that falls to the right; let it reach wide. Then 寸: a long horizontal, a vertical that ends in a hook to the left, and one dot. Watch the eighth stroke, the horizontal of 寸. It is the widest line in the character and it carries the whole upper part like a tray. The weight above is to the right, and the hook and dot below answer it on the left.

questions.claim: Your body is nearer to you than your name, and counts for more than your goods.
prompts: Answer the passage’s question honestly: on an ordinary day, which do you serve first?
When did you first learn that your name, your standing with others, could be lost? What did you start to do then?
Take the opposite: a good name outlasts the body, and some things are worth the body’s cost. What have you gladly spent yourself on?
Which side embarrasses you a little? Why might that be the one to look at?

questions.claim: The more extreme the attachment, the greater the cost; the bigger the hoard, the heavier the loss.
prompts: Do you agree, or does this sound like fear of loving anything fully?
What do you hold most tightly? Trace the grip back: what earlier loss does it remember?
Now hold the other view: only what you love without measure is worth having, and its cost is the proof. What feelings come?
Do you admire people who hold on or people who travel light? What do you say about the other kind when they are not present?

questions.claim: A person who knows what is enough, and when to stop, meets no disgrace and can last.
prompts: Has stopping in time ever protected you? Has it ever cost you something that you still want?
How do you know that you have had enough: of work, of food, of praise? Is the signal in the body or in a rule?
Suppose the opposite: those who do not say “enough” are the ones who change things, and to last long is not the highest aim. Stay with that. What stirs?
Which do you fear more, going too far or stopping too soon? Where does that fear come from?
